lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.intro: Spaniards greet warmly and don't rush it — a quick, friendly exchange before getting to business is the norm, not small talk to skip.
lessons.didYouKnow: The double cheek kiss (starting on the LEFT cheek) is standard between women, and between a man and a woman, even on a first meeting — but two men usually just shake hands unless they're close friends or family.
commonMistakes: Treating a greeting as a formality to rush through — Spaniards generally expect a beat of real warmth, even in a quick shop interaction.

quiz.question: Which cheek do you start on for the traditional Spanish greeting kiss?

lessons.title: Emergency Phrases
lessons.intro: A few phrases worth having ready before you land, just in case.
lessons.didYouKnow: Spain's general emergency number is 112, same as the rest of the EU — it works from any phone, even without a SIM card or credit.
commonMistakes: Not knowing 112 works even on a phone with no active plan or signal from your home carrier — worth remembering if your phone otherwise shows no service.

quiz.question: What's the general emergency number in Spain?

lessons.title: Tapas & Dining Culture
lessons.intro: Spanish meal times run much later than most visitors expect — and tapas culture has its own etiquette around ordering and sharing.
lessons.didYouKnow: Dinner in Spain often doesn't start until 9 or 10pm, and restaurants may not even open for dinner before 8pm — showing up at 6pm expecting a full dinner service is a classic tourist miss.
commonMistakes: Showing up for dinner at 6-7pm expecting a full restaurant experience — many kitchens aren't even open yet.
Tipping heavily like in the US — rounding up or leaving small change is normal; large tips aren't expected.

quiz.question: When do most Spaniards typically eat dinner?
Is heavy American-style tipping expected in Spain?

lessons.title: Siesta & Store Hours
lessons.intro: Especially outside big cities, plenty of shops still close for a few hours in the afternoon — worth planning around rather than being caught out by.
lessons.didYouKnow: Many small shops close from roughly 2pm to 5pm for "siesta" and then reopen into the evening — big-city chain stores and malls usually stay open through, but neighborhood shops often don't.
commonMistakes: Assuming every shop follows big-city hours — in smaller towns especially, a closed door at 3pm is completely normal, not a sign something's wrong.

quiz.question: What's a common reason a small Spanish shop might be closed mid-afternoon?

lessons.title: Metro & Transportation
lessons.intro: Spain's metro and rail systems are extensive and efficient — a few local habits will help you blend in and avoid fines.
lessons.didYouKnow: Ticket inspectors do random checks on metro and regional trains, and riding without a validated ticket can mean an on-the-spot fine even if you genuinely intended to pay.
commonMistakes: Boarding without a valid, validated ticket assuming you can pay later if asked — inspectors treat this as fare evasion, not an honest mistake.

quiz.question: What happens if a ticket inspector finds you without a valid ticket on the metro?
options: Nothing, you can pay them directly at full price
You can be fined on the spot

lessons.title: Nightlife Culture
lessons.intro: Spanish nightlife runs on a schedule that surprises most first-time visitors — bars and clubs don't really get going until well after most other countries have called it a night.
lessons.didYouKnow: It's completely normal for clubs ("discotecas") to not fill up until 2am, with some staying open until 6am — going out at 10-11pm, as you might elsewhere, means arriving to a mostly empty venue.
commonMistakes: Showing up to a club at 10-11pm expecting a full crowd — the real energy usually doesn't start until after midnight.

quiz.question: When do Spanish clubs typically get busy?
options: They don't — Spain has no club culture
